# Build a Shared Alexa+ Chore Chart That Rotates Weekly by Voice

> **In short:** You will build a household chore list in Alexa+, write a simple weekly rotation, and use your voice to ask who has which chore and to mark items done. Alexa+ cannot rotate chores on its own, so you update the rotation each week, and some features may depend on your plan or region.

This guide is for households that share chores and want less nagging. By the end, anyone in the home can ask Alexa+ what's on the chart, check off a chore, and get a reminder each Monday to move the assignments forward. You will also use a planning conversation with Alexa+ to draft the rotation, which is a useful habit for any multi-step task.

## Before you start
- **Assumed:** you already have an Amazon account, use Alexa+ on an Echo device or the Alexa app, and know how to start a conversation and send a request.
- **Who can use it:** Alexa+ access depends on your region and may require a Prime membership or a paid plan. Check Amazon's official Alexa page for current details before you rely on it.
- **Time:** about 25 minutes, plus a few seconds each Monday.
- **Household:** each person who will ask questions should have access to the same Alexa device or the shared lists. Lists are not always shared automatically, so check that in step 1.

## Step 1 — Create a shared Chores list

Start by making a list that everyone in the house can see. Either say "Alexa, create a list called Chores" to your Echo device, or open the Alexa app and look for a section named **Lists** (it may appear on the home screen or inside a menu). Tap the option to add a new list, and name it **Chores**. You should see an empty list with a text box or a "+" button for new items.

Next, add three chores by typing or saying them one at a time: "Dishes," "Trash and recycling," and "Bathroom." After each item is added, Alexa or the app confirms it by showing it on the list. Keep the names short so they are easy to say out loud later.

💬 Example: say "Alexa, add Dishes to my Chores list," then repeat for the other two.

If you don't see a Lists section, try asking Alexa+ "Show me my lists" to find where the feature lives on your device. If your household members can't see the list, look in the list's settings for a sharing or household option; the exact wording varies.

You'll know it worked when "Chores" appears in your lists and shows all three items.

## Step 2 — Draft the rotation with Alexa+

Now you need a rule for who does what. Ask Alexa+ to help you plan it, rather than doing the math in your head. Open a conversation and describe your people, your chores, and the rule you want. Keep your request specific: the more detail you give, the easier the reply is to use. Read the answer carefully, because Alexa+ may make arithmetic mistakes or pick a pattern you didn't intend.

Then create a second list called **Rotation** and add one line per week for the next three weeks, using the names from the answer. Each line should say who takes which chore, such as "Week 1: Sam dishes, Priya trash, Leo bathroom." Check that every person has each chore at least once in the cycle.

💬 Example prompt: "Plan a weekly chore rotation for three people: Sam, Priya and Leo. The chores are Dishes, Trash and Bathroom. Each week, everyone moves to the next chore. Show weeks 1 to 3 as a short list, one line per week."

If Alexa+ gives you an answer that is confusing or wrong, reply with a correction, such as "Priya should not have Bathroom twice in a row. Fix week 2." This follow-up pattern, where each new message builds on the previous answer, is the most useful habit in this guide.

You'll know it worked when your Rotation list has three clear weeks and each person's chore changes from one week to the next.

## Step 3 — Ask who has which chore by voice

With both lists ready, test the voice side. Anyone in the household can ask about this week's assignments. Try a question that names the list, such as "Alexa, what's on my Chores list?" Then ask a second question about the rotation, such as "Alexa, what's the rotation for week 2?" Alexa+ should read the item or line back to you.

Notice how the answer sounds. If it reads all three chores without saying who has which, your list is missing names. Go back to Step 2 and add the name to each line, like "Dishes: Sam this week."

💬 Example: "Alexa, what's the rotation for week 2?"

If Alexa+ reads the wrong list or says it doesn't understand, repeat the request with the list name, for example "from my Rotation list." Speak at a normal pace and wait for Alexa to finish before asking the next question.

You'll know it worked when Alexa+ answers out loud with a name and a chore, not just a list of words.

## Step 4 — Mark chores done by voice

Once someone finishes a chore, they should be able to mark it off without touching a screen. Say something like "Alexa, mark Dishes as done on my Chores list." On many shopping and to-do lists, Alexa moves the item to a completed section or crosses it off. The exact behavior depends on your device and app version, so look for a completed or checked section in the list view.

If Alexa+ cannot check an item off, you can still remove it or add a note like "Dishes done, Sam, Monday." This keeps the record readable even if the marking feature behaves differently in your setup. Remember that completed items may be cleared or hidden at some point, so don't rely on them as a permanent history.

💬 Example: "Alexa, mark Trash and recycling as done."

If it asks which list you mean, say the full name, "Chores." If it asks you to confirm, answer "yes" and wait for the confirmation.

You'll know it worked when the item disappears from the active list, or moves to a completed section you can see in the app.

## Step 5 — Set a Monday routine to start the rotation

Finally, make the chart run itself as a reminder. In the Alexa app, look for **Routines** (it may be under a menu or on the home screen). Create a new routine. Choose a **schedule** trigger for Monday morning at a time that suits your household, then add an action that makes Alexa speak. Look for an option like "Alexa says," and type a short message.

Use a message that reminds people to act, such as: "It's chore rotation day. Ask me what's on the Chores list, then update the Rotation list for this week." Save the routine and give it a clear name like "Monday chore rotation." Routines typically run on the device you choose, so pick the Echo in the room where everyone gathers.

💬 Example message: "Chore rotation day. Ask me who has which chore this week."

If you don't see Routines, search for it in the app's search or ask Alexa+ "How do I make a routine?" If your app only offers different actions, pick the simplest speech or announcement option available.

You'll know it worked when you can run the routine manually once and hear the message.

## Common mistakes
- **Expecting Alexa+ to rotate chores automatically.** It can't track who did what or move names around by itself. The fix is to update the Rotation list each Monday, or ask Alexa+ to draft next week's version using last week's list as input.
- **Using vague chore names.** "Clean" or "Help" is hard to say and hard to track. Use specific names like "Dishes" or "Bathroom sink" so the voice requests work reliably.
- **Trusting the math without checking.** AI-written plans can repeat a chore or skip a person. Read the three weeks aloud once, and correct any mistake with a follow-up message.

**What Alexa+ cannot do:** it cannot confirm that a chore was done well, enforce the schedule, or replace a conversation with the people sharing the work. It is a reminder and record-keeping tool.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** a family or roommates can share one chore chart, ask "who has the trash this week?" from any room, and stop arguing about whose turn it is.
- **For your business or work:** the same pattern works for team duty rosters, such as a weekly on-call or cleaning schedule for a shared office.
- **If you want to go further:** try a two-step prompt, where you first ask Alexa+ to list the chores that take the most time, then ask it to balance the rotation so each person's load feels fair.

## Try it now
In the next two minutes, create a list called **Chores**, add one item, and ask Alexa "what's on my Chores list?" You'll have the core of your household chart running.
